source_text: Paenitentiam hoc genus hominum, quod et ipsi retro fuimus, caeci, sine domini lumine, natura tenus norunt passionem animi quandam esse quae veniat de offensa sententiae peioris. Ceterum a ratione eius tantum absunt, quantum ab ipso rationis auctore. Quippe res dei ratio; quia deus omnium conditor, nihil non ratione providit, disposuit, ordinavit, nihil non ratione tractari intellegique voluit. Igitur ignorantes quique deum rem quoque eius ignorent necesse est, quia nullus omnino thesaurus extraneis patet. Itaque universam vitae conversationem sine gubernaculo rationis transfretantes imminentem saeculo procellam vitare non norunt. Quam autem in paenitentiae actu irrationabiliter diversentur, vel uno isto satis erit expedire, cum illam etiam in bonis factis suis adhibent. Paenitet fidei, amoris, simplicitatis, patientiae, misericordiae, prout quid in ingratiam cecidit. Semetipsos exsecrantur, quia benefecerint, eamque maxime paenitentiae speciem quae optimis operibus irrogatur in corde figunt, meminisse curantes, ne quid boni rursus praestent; contra paenitentiae malorum levius incubant. Denique facilius per eandem delinquunt quam per eandem recte faciunt.
thought_title: The unreasoning repentance of those without God
orientation: Tertullian opens the treatise by describing how people who do not know God misuse repentance, applying it even to good deeds.
pass_a_gloss: This kind of men, which we ourselves also were in the past, blind, without the light of the Lord, know repentance by nature only, that it is a certain passion of the soul which comes from offense of a worse opinion. But they are as far from its reason as from the author of reason himself. Indeed reason is a thing of God; because God, the founder of all things, provided, disposed, ordered nothing without reason, willed nothing to be handled and understood without reason. Therefore whoever are ignorant of God must necessarily be ignorant of his thing also, because no treasure at all lies open to strangers. And so, crossing over the whole conduct of life without the helm of reason, they do not know how to avoid the storm threatening the age. But how irrationally they wander in the act of repentance, it will be enough to explain by this one thing, when they apply it even to their good deeds. They repent of faith, of love, of simplicity, of patience, of mercy, according as anything has fallen into disfavor. They curse themselves because they have done good, and they fix in their heart especially that kind of repentance which is inflicted on the best works, taking care to remember not to perform anything good again; on the contrary, they lie more lightly upon repentance of evils. Finally, they sin through the same thing more easily than they do right through the same thing.

choices.why: Renders the limiting force of 'tenus' (as far as nature goes, and no further), contrasting natural knowledge with knowledge from God's light.
Keeps the comparative force of 'peioris' and the sense of a judgment or opinion that has been offended, matching the source's abstract phrasing.

choices.english: reason is a thing of God
choices.why: Preserves the compact predicate structure and the possessive sense that reason belongs to God.

choices.english: no treasure at all lies open to strangers
choices.why: Keeps the metaphor of a treasure and the verb 'patet' (lies open), with 'omnino' rendered as 'at all' for emphasis.
rejected: no treasure is accessible to strangers

choices.why: Renders the idiom of falling into 'ingratia' (lack of favor) with a natural English equivalent that keeps the falling metaphor.
Keeps the physical metaphor of 'incumbo' (lie upon, press upon) and the comparative 'levius', showing their lighter treatment of repentance for evils.

pass_b_english: This kind of people—and we ourselves were once among them, blind, without the Lord's light—know repentance by nature only, as a certain passion of the soul that comes from the offense of a worse opinion. But they are as far from its reason as they are from the very author of reason. For reason is a thing of God, because God, the founder of all things, has provided, arranged, and ordered nothing without reason, and has willed nothing to be handled or understood without reason. Therefore whoever is ignorant of God must also be ignorant of God's things, because no treasure at all lies open to strangers. And so they cross the whole course of life without the helm of reason, and they do not know how to avoid the storm that hangs over the world.

How irrationally they wander in the act of repentance will be clear enough from this one point: they apply it even to their good deeds. They repent of faith, of love, of simplicity, of patience, of mercy, whenever anything has fallen into disfavor. They curse themselves because they have done good, and they fix in their hearts that kind of repentance especially which is inflicted on the best works, taking care to remember not to do anything good again. But they lie more lightly upon repentance for evils. In short, they sin more easily through the same repentance than they do right.
